sample://team-learning: A fictional classroom study followed eight student teams for six weeks. Teams that spent ten minutes each week discussing what worked, what failed, and what they would change completed more tasks and reported fewer repeated mistakes. The study was small and did not use random assignment, so the results show an association rather than proof of causation.
sample://clear-goals: A fictional survey of 120 students compared groups given broad instructions with groups given specific, measurable goals. Students with specific goals reported higher confidence and completed more of the assigned work. The survey relied on self-reported confidence and was conducted in one school, which limits generalization.
sample://small-experiments: A fictional workplace experiment asked employees to test one small process improvement each week. Participants generated many ideas, but only a minority were retained after four weeks. The authors argue that small experiments reduce the cost of trying new approaches, while noting that leadership support affected participation.
